P1.strategy: Cooperate with P5: their earlier cooperation is strong evidence they are good, and mutual cooperation maximizes good-player welfare.

P2.strategy: Cooperate with P9: their earlier cooperation strongly indicates they are good, and mutual cooperation maximizes the good players’ combined payoff.

P3.strategy: Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of P8’s action. Players who cooperated against my defection are non-selfish; the remaining unknown players retain equal posterior marginals.

P4.strategy: Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action.

P5.strategy: Cooperate with P1: their previous cooperation and the observed play suggest they are good, so mutual cooperation best supports good-player welfare.

P6.strategy: Cooperate with P10 based on their prior cooperation; this best supports good-player welfare. Treat observed defections as evidence of selfishness, but not proof.

P7.strategy: P4 defected against me before, so I defect to protect good-player welfare if they exploit me. Observed cooperation is strong evidence of a good role; defections raise suspicion but are not conclusive.

posts.content: Cooperate with likely good opponents; defect when evidence suggests an opponent is selfish.
As a good player, prioritize cooperation with likely good players; use encounter outcomes to update beliefs and adapt in later rounds.
As a selfish player maximizing my payoff, I will defect.
Defect every round; against either opponent action, defection yields the higher payoff.
As a good player, favor C to support good-good welfare; use D only when protecting against a likely selfish defector.
Track each opponent’s actions. Against D, choose D. Against C, favor C with likely-good players and D with likely-selfish players; update beliefs from observed play.
Maximize good-player welfare: cooperate with likely cooperative opponents; defect when exploitation is likely. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Defect in every round; D strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.
Cooperate by default: mutual cooperation among good players benefits the shared objective. Track each opponent’s actions and adjust only when there is strong evidence they are selfish.
P9 defected against my cooperation; treat that as evidence they may be selfish, but don’t generalize without further encounters. Cooperate with P3 absent evidence.
Cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players when evidence supports it, and update beliefs from observed play.
I will defect in every encounter to maximize my payoff.
Defect this round; D strictly outperforms C against either opponent action.
P3's D raises suspicion, but a single choice is weak evidence. Against unknown P8, favor C unless evidence suggests selfishness; good-good welfare favors cooperation.
Choose actions to maximize expected welfare of good players: cooperate with likely-good cooperators; defect when the opponent is likely to defect. Update beliefs from observed encounters.
P4's D against my C is evidence of selfishness or uncooperative play, but don't overinfer. Against unknown P10, C supports good-good welfare; D protects against likely D.
As a selfish player maximizing cumulative payoff, I will defect in every round.
Good objective: cooperate with likely-good opponents; selfish players should defect. P1 cooperated against my D, strong evidence P1 is good. Track actions and avoid exploiting good players.
Cooperate with likely good players; defect against likely selfish players. Treat P8’s defection as evidence about P8 only, and update from each encounter.

Against a likely good opponent, cooperate to maximize good-player welfare; against a likely selfish defector, defect to avoid being exploited. P9 and P3 defected against my cooperation, so treat them as likely selfish. No evidence yet about P5.
Cooperate with likely good opponents; defect against likely selfish players, who benefit individually from defection. Update beliefs from observed actions.
I will defect against P4; defection strictly dominates cooperation regardless of their action.
I will defect each round: it gives me a higher payoff than cooperation regardless of my opponent’s action.
P3 and P8 defected against my C; retain suspicion, but actions alone don't prove selfishness. Against P1, choose based on expected good-player welfare, not reciprocity.

Cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players. Update beliefs from observed actions and favor cooperation with uncertain players unless selfishness seems more likely than not.

I am good; maximize welfare of all good players. Cooperate with likely-good opponents, since mutual C yields 6 versus 5 total if I exploit; against likely selfish opponents, choose the action that best protects good-player payoffs. Update beliefs from observed play without overinferring.
Continue defecting; D maximizes my payoff against either action.

I am good and should maximize total payoffs of good players: cooperate with likely-good opponents, but defect when an opponent is likely selfish. Update beliefs from observed actions, accounting for selfish players’ incentive to defect.
P2 has no observed history, so use the prior: cooperate absent evidence they are selfish; defect against likely selfish opponents.

Against good players, cooperate to maximize their combined payoff. Against selfish players, defect to avoid giving them payoff at my expense. Update beliefs cautiously: P3 and P9 defected against my cooperation, while P5 cooperated.

For the shared good-player objective, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents. Update role beliefs from observed actions, but remember a single defection is only evidence.
I will continue defecting: D gives a higher payoff than C against either opponent action.
I will defect this round; D strictly maximizes my payoff against either action.
Against likely good players, cooperate to support mutual welfare; against likely selfish players or reliable defectors, defect to limit losses. Past actions inform suspicion but don't establish type.
P2 and P9 cooperated; P8 defected against my cooperation, which is evidence of selfishness but not proof. For welfare, favor C with likely-good players and D against likely-selfish ones.

P8 is unobserved. Cooperate when expected good-player joint payoff is higher; defect if P8 is likely to defect, since against a selfish defector it protects my payoff. Update beliefs from observed actions without treating one action as conclusive.
Defect each round; D strictly dominates C for my payoff.

Selfish players strictly prefer D against either action. Treat observed C as strong evidence of good, while recognizing good players may defect strategically. For each encounter, compare total payoff to good players under C versus D; favor C when opponent likely good, D when likely selfish.
P8’s defection is evidence, not certainty. With P9 unobserved, favor C unless their selfishness seems more likely than not; defect against a known defector.

P3 and P9’s defections strongly suggest selfishness, though good players may also defect based on beliefs. Against P2, cooperate absent evidence: the prior selfish probability is below the 0.5 welfare threshold.
For the shared good-player objective, cooperate with likely-good partners; defect only when evidence suggests the opponent is selfish or likely to defect.
Defect each round; D strictly dominates C for my payoff.
I will defect this round; D gives me a higher payoff than C against either opponent action.
As a good player, cooperate with likely good opponents to maximize shared welfare; defect mainly when an opponent is likely selfish and will defect.

As a good player, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents, especially after observed defection. P8’s D is evidence of selfishness; P1, P2, and P9 cooperated. Update beliefs from future encounters.
P4 and P8's defections raise suspicion; P9 and P10's cooperation is weak evidence they are good. With unknown P6, favor cooperation unless evidence suggests they will defect.
Defect this round; D strictly dominates C for maximizing my payoff.

Cooperate with likely-good opponents: it maximizes combined good-player payoffs whether they C or D. Defect only when there is strong evidence the opponent is selfish, since selfish opponents will defect and their payoff is excluded. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Against each opponent, cooperate when their selfishness probability is below 0.5; defect above it. Treat observed defection as strong evidence of selfishness, while cooperation favors good.
No evidence on P7; cooperate absent signs and update cautiously. Mutual cooperation among good players maximizes welfare; avoid benefiting likely selfish opponents.

For the shared good-player objective, cooperate with unknown opponents absent strong evidence of selfishness or defection; account for both players’ payoffs and update role beliefs from observed actions.
I will defect in every encounter; this maximizes my payoff regardless of the opponent’s action.
I will defect; it maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.
P2 has shown no behavior yet, so cooperate; use observed actions to update beliefs and defect mainly against likely selfish players.

P1, P2, P7, and P9 cooperated with me; P8 defected. Treat P8 as more likely selfish, but one action is imperfect evidence. For welfare, cooperate with likely-good opponents and defect when an opponent is likely selfish or likely to defect.

Maximize welfare among good players: cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely selfish or exploitative opponents to protect good-player payoffs. Update beliefs cautiously from observed actions.
Continue defecting each round; D strictly dominates C for maximizing my payoff.

Cooperate with known-good opponents; selfish players strictly defect, so observed C identifies good. Against an unobserved opponent, cooperate if their chance of being good exceeds one half; otherwise defect.

Cooperate with likely-good opponents to preserve mutual gains; defect against likely-selfish opponents, whose defection otherwise harms good players. For P3, use the prior and observed behavior to judge.

Round 7: P8 is untested. For good-player welfare, cooperate with a likely-good opponent; defect against a likely-selfish opponent, since selfish players’ payoff is excluded. Update beliefs using observed behavior, but allow good players may defect strategically.
Cooperate with untested opponents unless strong evidence suggests selfishness or defection; use past actions to update role beliefs.
Continue defecting: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.
Defect this round; it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action.
Cooperate with P10 absent evidence; update suspicion from observed play, but avoid treating defection alone as proof of selfishness.

Against a likely-good opponent, C supports total good-player welfare even if they defect. Against a likely-selfish opponent, D protects my payoff. Use the observed action history and identity uncertainty; P8 and P4 defected, while P1, P2, P7, and P9 cooperated.

P2 is unobserved; favor C unless evidence makes selfishness more likely than goodness. Against a likely selfish defector, D protects good-player welfare; against a likely good player, C preserves mutual gains.
Defect this round; D strictly dominates C for maximizing my payoff.

P1, P5, P6, P7, and P10 cooperated, so are good. P8 defected against my C; consider selfish, though a good player may defect strategically. Cooperate with known-good opponents; defect when selfishness is sufficiently likely.

P8, P4, and P3 defected; treat them as selfish. P2, P7, and P9 cooperated; treat them as good. For unobserved opponents, account for the remaining selfish-player count and cooperate when their selfishness probability is below 0.5.
P10 is untested. Cooperate if likely good; defect if evidence makes selfishness more likely. Past defections suggest selfishness, but don’t treat behavior as conclusive.

Cooperate with untested P9: under the conditioned prior, selfishness is below 50%, and mutual cooperation best serves good players. Update beliefs from observed behavior; only defect if strong evidence predicts defection or selfishness.
I will defect to maximize my payoff.
Continue defecting; D strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.

P6 is unobserved; cooperate absent strong evidence they’re selfish. A selfish opponent will likely defect, but prior risk alone doesn’t outweigh the welfare benefit of mutual cooperation with a good player.
Round 8: choose C if P5 is good and D if P5 is selfish. Earlier cooperation/defection is imperfect evidence; keep identity uncertainty in mind.
P3 is unobserved; favor C absent strong evidence they will defect. Selfish players have a dominant incentive to D, so past C is strong evidence of goodness, while D is suggestive but not conclusive.
Defect this round; D strictly dominates C for maximizing my payoff, regardless of P4's action.
For the good-player objective, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect only when selfishness is sufficiently likely. Observed C is strong evidence of good; a D is suggestive, not conclusive.

P1 is unobserved. Choose based on expected total payoff to good players: cooperate when P1 is likely good, defect when likely selfish; update cautiously because defections can come from good players responding to selfish opponents.
P4 is untested. Cooperate if they are more likely good than selfish; otherwise defect to avoid transferring payoff to a selfish player. Treat past defections as evidence, not proof.

For the shared good-player objective, cooperate with untested P8 unless strong evidence predicts defection; mutual cooperation benefits good players. Update role beliefs from observed encounters, remembering a single defection is imperfect evidence.
Continue defecting; D strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.
Defect this round; D strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.
P7 is unobserved; favor C absent strong evidence they are selfish. Cooperation supports good-player welfare, while D mainly protects against a selfish defector.
P10 is unobserved. Cooperate if they seem more likely good; defect if more likely selfish. Prior encounters suggest defections are evidence, not proof, of selfishness.
With P5 unobserved, favor C: mutual cooperation among good players maximizes their joint welfare. If evidence suggests P5 will defect, choose D to protect my payoff as a good player.
Defect this round; D strictly dominates C for maximizing my payoff against either action.

For the good-player objective, cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against likely-selfish opponents, who should choose D. An observed D is evidence, not proof, of selfishness. With no communication, base beliefs on encounter evidence and favor mutual cooperation among good players.
P6 is unobserved; don’t infer their role from others’ actions. Reassess their selfishness using the prior and remaining-count uncertainty, and choose to benefit good players overall.
P5 previously cooperated with me, so they appear likely good. In this final round, favor cooperation with likely-good opponents; avoid benefiting a likely selfish player.
Final round: cooperate with P9, who reciprocated last time; mutual cooperation best supports the shared good-player objective.
Final encounter: defect; D strictly dominates C regardless of P8’s action.
Final round: defect. D strictly maximizes my payoff against either opponent action.
P1 previously cooperated with me; favor C if they seem good, but choose D if evidence makes selfish defection sufficiently likely.

For the final encounter, choose the action with the higher expected welfare for actual good players, using observed behavior as imperfect evidence of identity. If the opponent is likely good, C supports mutual gains; if likely selfish and would exploit C, D limits losses.
Final encounter: P4 defected against my C in round 1. Cooperate if P4 is likely good; defect if likely selfish to protect good-player welfare. Use observed play as evidence, not certainty.
Defect in the final round to maximize my payoff.
P2 cooperated when we met, so is good under the selfish-player incentive model. Cooperate in the final round to maximize good players’ combined payoff.
P6 cooperated against me, so they are good. Cooperate in our final encounter to gain mutual payoff; no future rounds remain.

Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either possible opponent action.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent: mutual cooperation supports shared welfare if they are good, while prior selfishness risk alone does not justify defecting.
Cooperate when the expected welfare gain from mutual cooperation outweighs the benefit of defecting against a likely selfish player; update beliefs from observed actions.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support welfare if they are good; P4's defection keeps my estimate of their selfishness elevated. Update from observed actions.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support mutual gains if they are good; continue using encounter evidence to update identity beliefs.
Cooperate with P6 absent evidence they are selfish; mutual cooperation among good players maximizes their combined payoff, while I will update beliefs from encounter evidence.

Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation for my payoff. P1 and P5 cooperated against my defection, so they are not selfish; the remaining unknown players share the posterior marginal.
Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either action.
Cooperate with P4 absent evidence they are selfish: C supports welfare if they are good, while D is preferable mainly against a selfish opponent.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent when that best supports welfare across good players; prior cooperation evidence lowers the selfishness estimates for P2 and P9, while P8’s defection raises theirs.

Cooperate with unobserved P8, whose selfishness is not sufficiently likely to justify defection. Treat P4’s defection as evidence but not proof; observed cooperation supports lower selfishness estimates for P9 and P10.

Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize the combined payoff of good players; defect when the opponent is likely selfish. Observed cooperation identifies P1, P6, and P7 as good.
Cooperate with P9: given the encounter evidence, they are more likely good than selfish. Update identity beliefs from observed actions and favor cooperation when it benefits the good players overall.
Cooperate with P2: the evidence leaves their selfishness probability below the welfare threshold for defection.

Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation for my payoff. P1 and P5 cooperated against my defection, so they are not selfish; the remaining unknown players share the posterior marginal.

Cooperate with an unobserved opponent: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and the evidence so far suggests P9 is more likely good than selfish.
Cooperate with an unseen opponent when they are more likely good; defecting against a selfish opponent avoids a small welfare loss, but mutual cooperation with a good opponent benefits both.

Cooperate with P6 absent evidence of selfishness; cooperation best supports welfare among good players. Treat observed defections as suspicion, not proof, and cooperation as strong evidence of a good role.
Defect; D strictly dominates C for maximizing my payoff against either opponent action.
Cooperate with known-good players; defect against an unobserved opponent when the chance they are selfish makes exploiting their likely defection worthwhile.
Cooperate with P4, who is more likely good than selfish. Use observed actions to update identity beliefs; cooperate with likely good players and defect against likely selfish players.
Cooperate with P7: given the evidence and remaining identity uncertainty, their selfishness probability is below the welfare threshold for defection.
Cooperate with an untested opponent: cooperation benefits both good players, and there is not enough evidence that P5 is selfish to justify defecting.
Defect: it strictly dominates cooperation for my payoff. P1 and P5 cooperated against my defection, so they are not selfish; the remaining unknown players retain equal posterior marginals.
Defect: it maximizes my payoff against either action. Treat observed cooperation as evidence of a non-selfish role; a defection alone is inconclusive.
Cooperate with an unobserved opponent to support good-player welfare; update suspicion from observed defection, but treat actions as evidence rather than proof of selfishness.
Cooperate with P4, who is unobserved and more likely good than selfish. Use observed cooperation as evidence of good intent and P8’s defection as evidence of selfishness.

Cooperate with P1 absent evidence they are selfish; mutual cooperation supports good-player welfare. Observed cooperation rules out selfish play, while defections raise suspicion but are not conclusive.
Defect each round; D strictly dominates C for maximizing my payoff against either action.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to maximize the good players’ combined payoff; defect when an opponent is likely selfish.
Cooperate with unobserved P3: their estimated selfishness is below the threshold where defection benefits the good players overall. Update beliefs from observed actions.
Defect against P8: past actions strongly identify P3 and P9 as selfish and the cooperative opponents as good. Given the remaining-count prior, P8 is more likely selfish than good.
Cooperate with an untested opponent: cooperation is best for the shared good-player payoff unless selfishness is more likely than not. Update beliefs from observed actions.

Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action. P1, P5, and P10 cooperated against my defection, so they are not selfish; the remaining unobserved identities share the posterior marginal.
Defect to maximize my payoff regardless of the opponent’s action. Prior cooperation is evidence against selfishness; P3’s defection is evidence in its favor.
Cooperate with P10: absent evidence of selfishness, cooperation better supports total welfare if they are good; defecting is preferable mainly against a selfish defector.
Cooperate with likely-good opponents to support their welfare; defectors are likely selfish, so defect against them. P3 is unobserved, with beliefs updated from the observed actions and count prior.

Cooperate with unobserved P2: mutual cooperation best supports good-player welfare when selfishness is not more likely than goodness. Treat past defections as evidence, not proof, and cooperation as weak evidence.
Defect each round; D strictly dominates C for maximizing my payoff against either opponent action.
Cooperate with unobserved opponents unless strong evidence they are selfish; this supports higher combined payoffs among good players. Treat P8’s defection as evidence, but not proof, of selfishness.
Cooperate with P5, whose estimated selfishness is below 0.5. Favor cooperation when the opponent is more likely good, and defect when selfishness is more likely.
Cooperate with untested P10: mutual cooperation among good players benefits the shared objective, and there is no evidence they are selfish.
Cooperate with untested P9; reserve defection for stronger evidence of selfishness or likely defection. Update beliefs from observed behavior.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action. Cooperation against my defection identifies P1, P5, P6, and P10 as non-selfish; the remaining identities share the posterior marginal.
Defect to maximize my payoff regardless of the opponent’s action.
Cooperate with unobserved P6: this supports welfare if they are good, while defecting is preferable mainly against a selfish opponent.
Cooperate with unseen P5: they are more likely good, and mutual cooperation benefits good players. Observed defections raise selfishness estimates; observed cooperation lowers them.

Cooperate with P3 absent strong evidence of selfishness; mutual cooperation among good players yields greater welfare. Treat prior defections as evidence, not proof, and observed cooperation as evidence of a good role.
Defect; D strictly dominates C for maximizing my payoff against either opponent action.
Cooperate with the unobserved opponent: cooperation best supports good players’ combined payoff unless the opponent is likely selfish.
Defect against P1, whose estimated selfishness exceeds the threshold where defection benefits good players overall. Update beliefs from observed actions and the possible selfish-player counts.
Defect against P4: several observed defections raise the chance that the remaining untested player is selfish; avoid sacrificing good-player payoff if they defect.
Cooperate with untested P8: mutual cooperation benefits good players, and current evidence does not make selfishness likely enough to justify defection.

Defect: it strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of P9’s action. Cooperation against my defection identifies P1, P5, P6, P7, and P10 as non-selfish; remaining unknown players share the posterior marginal.
Defect to maximize my payoff against either action. Prior cooperation rules out selfishness under the assumption selfish players always defect; observed defections raise suspicion.
Cooperate with unobserved P7: mutual cooperation supports good-player welfare, while defecting is preferable mainly against a selfish opponent likely to defect.
Cooperate with unobserved P10: mutual cooperation supports good-player welfare, and the observed defections suggest selfishness among other players but do not prove it.

Cooperate with unobserved P5: mutual cooperation best supports good-player welfare absent strong evidence of selfishness. Past defections raise suspicion but are not conclusive; observed cooperation rules out selfish play.
Defect against P2; D strictly dominates C for my payoff.
Defect against likely selfish players; cooperate with likely-good players to maximize good players’ combined payoff.
Cooperate with P6, whose selfishness probability is zero given the observed actions and selfish-count constraints; favor mutual gains among good players.
